章节.A Line That Never Materialized:
During the Hiroshima Gas and Electric era, a railway line connecting Hiroshima City and Kure City was planned. An application was submitted on December 20, 1919 (Taisho 8). According to the plan, the terminal on the Kure side was to be located near Mitsuda Bridge. Additionally, a patent application for laying a tramline along Hon-dori was made. At that time, however, it was rejected due to being a competing line to the government railway (Kure Line). Subsequently, the line was shortened and changed to run between Hiroshima and Funakoshi, and a license was obtained on February 18, 1926 (Taisho 15). Although the initial plan for the southern route was intended for commuter transport to the Hiroshima Plant of Nippon Seiko, it was abandoned because it would have obstructed the passage of riverboats. After that, the planned northern route, which would have competed with the government railway, had its applications repeatedly submitted, but requests to delay construction were rejected. The license expired on August 5, 1931 (Showa 6). An application was also made to lay a line from Den-miya-jima Station (present-day Hiroden Miyajimaguchi Station) to Iwakuni City in Yamaguchi Prefecture, but a license was never obtained.

Furthermore, there was no route plan from Yokokawa to Kōda-chō (present-day Aki Takada-shi).
Additionally, in the 1927 (Showa 2) publication "The Construction of Greater Hiroshima" by the Hiroshima Chamber of Commerce and Industry, routes were proposed: a line extending the Yokokawa Line to Eba (later realized as the Eba Line); a line passing through Tokobamachi and Danbaramachi to reach Takano Bridge (later realized as the Minami Line); a line from Kibi passing through Kannon Bridge, Sumiyoshi Bridge, and Takano Bridge to reach Danbaramachi; a line from Yokokawa passing through Shirajima to reach Hiroshima Station; and a line from Sarukō Bridge passing through Onagachō to reach Fuchū. In response to these proposals, Hiroshima Gas Electric Railway created blueprints and conducted studies, but most of them were never realized.

During the war, in July 1945 (Showa 20), a patent was obtained for transporting Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Hiroshima Machinery Works workers between Tenma-cho and Shōwa Shinkai (present-day Kan'on Shinkai) (approximately 3 km). Materials were supplied by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, and the project was funded by the single-tracking of the Shirajima Line. However, in August of the same year, the Hiroshima city tramways suffered catastrophic damage due to the atomic bombing of Hiroshima City, and construction could not begin. In 1959 (Showa 34), an application to abandon the project was filed, and the patent expired.
章节.Relocation of Tracks Due to Land Readjus:
On August 6, 1949 (Showa 24), the Hiroshima Peace Memorial City Construction Law was enacted. Accordingly, the Ministry of Construction and the Hiroshima City Reconstruction Bureau held consultations and formulated a plan. The plan called for widening roads and moving the tracks to the center of the road, which would have required relocating more than half of the 18.4 km of the then-existing city lines—9.4 km.
Regarding the cost-sharing for the track relocation, the initial plan had called for a 1:3 split, but after a reassessment, by 1952 (Showa 27), the average burden had risen to approximately 48%, with a maximum of 57%. Due to petitions to reduce Hiroden's share, the burden was later limited to the tramway facilities alone. By 1954 (Showa 29), the Inari Ohashi-Hiroshima Station section had a burden of 22.4%.
The relocation of the tracks to the center of the road and the associated track work were carried out in stages: the track relocation around Sakanmachi (present-day Motokawa-cho) was completed in 1956 (Showa 31), and the relocation of the Kanon-cho-Ki section, which became obsolete due to the Ota River Diversion Channel and the abandonment of the Fukushima River, was completed in 1964 (Showa 39).

Construction began in 1947 (Showa 22) as a project of Hiroshima City, starting the replacement of tracks alongside the road. Within Hiroshima City, there were seven bridges shared by Hiroshima Electric Railway tracks (Arakami Bridge, Inari Ohashi Bridge, Aioi Bridge, Hiroden Tenma Bridge, Shinkibi Bridge, Mikou Bridge, and Yokokawa Shimbashi Bridge); among these, Hiroden Tenma Bridge was not on an urban planning road. Except for Arakami Bridge, which had been a combined-use bridge since before World War II, the other five bridges required either replacement or new construction. In 1950 (Showa 25), Inari Ohashi Bridge was completed; in 1958 (Showa 33), Yokokawa Shimbashi Bridge; in 1964 (Showa 39), Shinkibi Bridge was completed in conjunction with the completion of the Ota River Diversion Channel; in 1983 (Showa 58), Aioi Bridge; and in 1990 (Heisei 2), Mikou Bridge.

The track replacement spanned a long period, with the final sections—the Kōmachi–Funairi Honmachi section and the Tokaichi–Teramachi section—completed in 1995 (Heisei 7). It took more than 40 years to complete the entire project.

章节.Construction of the Ekimae Ohashi Line a:
On June 29, 2010 (Heisei 22), Hidenobu Ochi assumed the position of president. Prior to his appointment, on May 12, he had proposed a new streetcar route, the "Ekimae Ohashi Line," connecting JR Hiroshima Station with Inaricho, Minami-ku, Hiroshima City, aiming to begin operations between 2016 and 2017 to make access easier.
Subsequently, regarding the boarding method, the JR side included an elevated boarding area in the Hiroshima Station redevelopment plan, while Hiroden expressed a preference for an underground boarding area. Later, in January 2013, following President Ochi's dismissal, the policy was reviewed, and on the 18th of that month, the president announced a shift in policy to an elevated system.

The "Hiroshima Station South Exit Plaza Reorganization Basic Policy Study Committee," composed of academic experts and other individuals, was established in Hiroshima City. Its first meeting was held on August 31, 2010 (Heisei 22), and studies were conducted, including the section from the streetcar's Ekimae Ohashi station onward. In June 2013, the study committee reached a consensus in favor of an "elevated structure" plan. From August 2013 (Heisei 25) to May 2014 (Heisei 26), four resident explanation meetings were held. Under the initial proposal, the existing section of the main line between Hiroshima Station and Inaricho, which detoured eastward near the station front, would be abolished. A new track would be constructed from Inaricho through Ekimae Ohashi. The plan was to ascend onto an elevated structure at Ekimae Ohashi and enter the Hiroshima Station building. Additionally, connecting the Minami Line to the Ekimae Ohashi section via Tokabacho was deemed difficult. Consequently, the Minami Line would instead run from the Hiyamacho intersection (between Hiyamashita and Danbara-ichome) through the Matsukawacho intersection.

The route is scheduled to be changed to connect from Inaricho Ni to the area in front of the station via Ohashi. In conjunction with this change, the section of the main line between Inaricho and Hiroshima Station, as well as the section of the Minami Line between Hijiyamacho Intersection and Tokobacho, will be closed. The three tram stops—Sarukobashicho, Tokobacho, and Danbara-ichome—on both sections will be abolished, and plans are in place to establish new tram stops in the Matsukawacho area to replace Tokobacho and Danbara-ichome. Furthermore, as a remedial measure for residents near the abolished tram stops, it is planned to operate replacement buses via Hiroshima Station as the starting point, using routes such as Hiroden Bus. However, there have been many objections from local residents regarding the abolition of the tram stops and the operation of replacement buses (for instance, if the bus route starts at Hiroshima Station, transferring is unavoidable when heading toward the commercial areas of Hatchobori and Kamiyamacho). As a result, the Hiroshima City side has decided to continue its deliberations. Additionally, at the third local explanation meeting held in January 2014, discussions were held on how to address the objections.

Regarding the case where the existing Minami Line is retained up to Tobamachi Streetcar Stop, it was confirmed that, in terms of traffic safety for both streetcars and automobiles and the convenience of signal operations, it is difficult to install a branch point at the Ekimae Ohashi South End Intersection, which would become the intersection with the Ekimae Ohashi Line. In addition, a proposal was made to install tracks at the Inaricho Intersection to allow turning from the Tobamachi direction toward Hiroshima Station (specifically, from Hijiayama to Danbara 1-chome to Tobamachi to Inaricho to Hiroshima Station); however, this was judged to be difficult due to the passing distance at the Inaricho Intersection.
In March 2014, the neighborhood associations along the route, who had opposed the abolition of the streetcar stops between Tobamachi and Danbara 1-chome, submitted a request for the construction of a new loop line including both of these stops. As a result of the verification, it was determined that this could be realized, since, in this case, no obstacles would arise in terms of signaling or traffic safety by newly constructing and maintaining tracks from the main line's Inaricho direction to the Minami Line's Danbara 1-chome direction at the Tobamachi Intersection.

If that becomes the case, both tram stops will remain, and it will no longer be possible to go directly to Hiroshima Station. As for what can be done regarding direct travel toward Hatchobori and Kamiyamacho, residents generally have a favorable impression. Furthermore, at the time of consideration by the City of Hiroshima, transportation systems circulating through the city center were primarily buses such as “Meipuru~Pu,” which were intended mainly for tourists. Therefore, it was judged that opening a circular tram line would increase visitor circulation and contribute to revitalizing the city. On the other hand, although the Sarukobashi-cho tram stop will be abolished, bus stops in the surrounding area will be consolidated in locations immediately accessible from the former Sarukobashi-cho tram stop, thereby ensuring convenience for the vicinity of the relevant tram stops. The proposal to operate replacement buses has thus been abandoned.

After that, through discussions and study committees with JR West and Hiroshima Electric Railway, on September 2, 2014, the “Basic Policy on the Reorganization of the Hiroshima Station South Exit Plaza, etc.” was announced. This included proposals for a circular route, the newly established Matsukawa-cho tram stop (which was originally scheduled for closure), and the expansion of Inari-cho.

On March 27, 2019, Hiroshima Electric Railway officially announced its policy to improve the Haekimae-Ohashi Loop Route and the Bi Loop Route. Following the proposal published by Hiroshima City in 2014, the plan includes constructing a new loop route between “Hiroshima Station – (Haekimae-Ohashi) – Inaricho – (provisional name) Matsukawacho – Hijiyama,” abolishing the section of the main line between “Hiroshima Station – Sarukenchō – Tokobachō” by routing it via Haekimae-Ohashi, and additionally constructing a new loop route between “Kamiyamachō – Hatchōbori – Tokobachō – Danbara-ichichōme – Minamimachi-rokuchōme – City Hall Mae – Kamiyamachō.” In conjunction with this, the plan incorporates the construction of new tracks near Tokobachō (toward Inaricho ⇔ Danbara-ichichōme) and the consolidation of streetcar stops. Hiroshima Electric Railway filed a patent application based on the Railway Act in April 2019, and since then, aims to begin construction in fiscal year 2020 and open the route in spring 2025.
章节.The Era of Hiroshima Electric Railway:
As the number of residents increased, in order to solve the problem of infectious diseases caused by sewage flowing into the moats of Hiroshima Castle, a decision to fill in the moats was made in 1908 (Meiji 41). This decision served as the catalyst for four applications for railway construction. Ultimately, due to prior negotiations, the competition between two companies—“Hiroshima Electric Railway,” backed by Tokyo-based capital and involving Miya Hiroji, Fukuzawa Momosuke, and Matsunaga Zaoemon—and “Hiroshima Electric Tramway,” established by Osaka-based capital including Obayoshi Yoshigoro and Kataoka Naoki—was resolved. On February 7, 1910 (Meiji 43), the latter obtained licenses to construct the following lines: Hiroshima Station–Kibi (currently part of the Main Line), Dobashi–Nakashima-Shinbashi–Takano Bridge–Mikuni Bridge (currently part of the Ujina Line), Hachobori–Takeyamacho–Mikuni Bridge (never realized), and Tokaichi–Yokokawa (currently the Yokokawa Line). On June 18 of the same year, the company was established with a capital of 3 million yen. Subsequently, the route between Hachobori–Takeyamacho–Mikuni Bridge was changed to pass through Kayamachi, and a new license was obtained for the Hachobori–Shirajima (currently the Shirajima Line) line. In July 1911 (Meiji 44), the first phase of track construction began.

It begins. In November 1911, the filling of the outer moat of the castle was completed, and in the following year, 1912 (Taisho 1), the filling of the Nishitogawa River was finished as a canal. After that, Aioi-dori and Koi-jo-dori were developed.
Regarding the Miyajima Line, even before the Hiroshima Electric Railway submitted its application, there had been a route plan from Koi to the fish market all the way to Kusatsu. In 1910 (Meiji 43), Hiroshima Electric Railway, along with Kusatsu Electric Railway and Saeki Light Railway, submitted an application based on the railway ordinance, but it was rejected due to competition with the government railway (Sanyo Main Line). On December 8, 1916 (Taisho 5), Miyajima Electric Railway submitted a patent application and it was accepted, but the negotiations with the relevant towns and villages failed, and the plan was ultimately abandoned.

In November 1912 (Taisho 1), the section from present-day Ujina Line's Hiroshima Station Front, via Kamiyamacho, to present-day Hakushima Line's Gokoku Bridge, and the section from present-day Hakushima Line's Hatchobori to Hakushima were opened. To commemorate the opening, 50 cars of the 100 series (A series) (car numbers 101-150) were prepared. The following month, the Kamiyamacho-Kofu section of the present-day Main Line was opened. In April 1915 (Taisho 4), the section from Gokoku Bridge East End to Ujina was opened. However, at that time, it was a single track, and a pedestrian connection was maintained from Gokoku Bridge to Gokoku Bridge East End.

章节.The Era of Hiroshima Gas Electric Railwa:
In August 1917 (Taisho 6), Hiroshima Electric Railway merged with Hiroshima Gas (now Hiroshima Gas), becoming Hiroshima Gas Electric Railway with a capital of 6 million yen. This was done to stabilize the company's financial structure by integrating the electric railway division, which had high sales during the summer, with the gas division, which had high sales during the winter.

The city line saw the opening of the Sakoncho–Mishino section, which would later become part of the current Yokokawa Line, in November 1917 (Taisho 6). In May 1919 (Taisho 8), the dedicated track bridge at Mikonomibashi was completed, connecting the Ujina Line as a single line. In 1921 (Taisho 10), ten cars that would later become the B-type (second-generation cars 101–110) were purchased from the Osaka Municipal Streetcar. Consequently, the original cars 101–150 were renumbered to 1–50. In April 1925 (Taisho 14), cars 151–160, which would later become the 150-type (E-type) and are currently the oldest fleet of Hiroden as of 2013, were introduced. Around June of the same year, following the example of the Miyajima Line cars, the characters “A” were added to the lower left side of the car bodies for the 0-type, “B” for the 100-type (second generation), and “E” for the 150-type. In 1927 (Showa 2), an additional 20 B-type cars (second-generation 100-type) were purchased from the Osaka Municipal Streetcar. In 1930 (Showa 5), ten G-type cars (later the first-generation 200-type) were introduced. In December 1935 (Showa 10), the line was relocated to a new double-track section between the eastern end of Mikonomibashi and Ujina. Between 1933 and 1934, the trolley poles were changed from two to one. In 1937 (Showa 12), a fire occurred at the Chida Depot. As a result of restoring the damaged cars, eleven 100-type (first generation) cars were converted into the 450-type. In 1938 (Showa 13)

) purchased five 300-series cars, which became the first bogie cars on the city tram lines from Osaka City Tram, and ten 23-series cars from Keio Electric Railway (now Keio Corporation), forming the 500-series (first generation). Additionally, all B-series cars were updated and became the 400-series.
Around the same time, with the enforcement of the City Planning Law (old law) in 1920 (Taisho 9), Hiroshima Prefecture established a road improvement plan for the city center. Entering the Showa period, the width of the electric railway right-of-way was expanded to 13 ken and a half (approximately 24.5 meters), and bridges were rebuilt as combined road and railway bridges. Hiroden also carried out successive upgrades, such as doubling its tracks. Notably, the funding for these projects came not only from prefectural bonds but was also partially covered by investment from Hiroden.

The Miyajima Line traces its origins to March 7, 1919 (Taisho 8), when Hiroshima Keiben Tetsudo obtained a license for the Kibi–Kusatsu section. On April 18 of the same year, the license was transferred to Hiroshima Gas Electric Railway. In June of that year, the company applied to the Railway Bureau to succeed the construction rights, apply for a license for the Kusatsu-machi–Oono-mura section, and change the power source from steam locomotives to electric power. These applications were approved on September 25, and construction of the Miyajima Line commenced on November 16. In August 1922 (Taisho 11), the first construction section of the Miyajima Line, between Kibi-machi and Kusatsu-machi, opened for service. Concurrently, in June of the same year, the C-type (later the 1000-type) cars were introduced. In April 1924 (Taisho 13), the second construction section, between Kusatsu-machi and Hatsukaichi-machi, was extended. Along with this extension, the D-type (later the 1010-type) cars were introduced in December 1923 (Taisho 12). In July 1925 (Taisho 14), the section between Hatsukaichi-machi and Jimigasaki opened. At the same time, the F-type (later the 1020-type) cars were introduced in that month. Concurrently, a connecting ferry service to Miyajima began operation. In July 1926 (Taisho 15), the section between Jimigasaki and Shin-Miyajima opened, connecting to the ferry service. In February 1931 (Showa 6), the section between Shin-Miyajima and Densha-Miyajima (present-day Hiroden-Miyajimaguchi) opened, completing the entire Miyajima Line. On the same day, the ferry service was discontinued. In addition, in 1930 (Showa 5), the H-type

The (later 1030 series) was introduced. In the 1937 (Showa 12) fire, one each of the C and D series, for a total of two cars, were damaged. Reusing their underframes and other components, they were restored in 1941 (Showa 16) as the semi-steel 1040 series.
In 1939 (Showa 14), the series names, which had been letters, were changed to numerical series names, similar to the car numbers.

章节.From Company Establishment to the Atomic:
At that time, due to the "No Country, No Policy" policy, on January 30, 1942 (Showa 17), a special shareholders' meeting approved the separation of the transportation division. On February 2 of the same year, applications were submitted to the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Ministry of Railways for permission to transfer the railway lines, and to the Ministry of Railways for permission to transfer the local railway, passenger motor transport business, and other operations. On April 4 of the same year, transfer permissions were granted for each transportation business, and on April 10, 1942 (Showa 17), the transportation business division of Hiroshima Gas Electric Railway was separated to become Hiroshima Electric Railway. In this year, the 600 series (first generation) and 650 series were introduced. In December 1943 (Showa 18), the section between Dobashi and Funairi Honmachi, which is now part of the Eboshi Line, opened. In June 1944 (Showa 19), the section between Funairi Honmachi and Funairi Minamimachi opened as a single track line. The following July, the section between Hatsukaichi and Densha Miyajima on the Miyajima Line was converted to single track. Using those tracks, the Minami Line opened in December. In March 1945 (Showa 20), the section between Funairi Honmachi and Funairi Minamimachi was doubled. Around this time, the current route network was almost completed.

Around that time, as there were technical advancements in current collection devices, starting in April 1940 (Showa 15), tests began on the Shirashima Line, with four 100-series cars equipped with viewgers and one 200-series car equipped with a pantograph. By August 1944 (Showa 19), all vehicles had been fitted with them. This replaced the trolley poles, which had become easy targets for enemy fire, and successfully led to the first full-scale practical application of viewgers in Japan. On the Miyajima Line as well, the current collection devices were changed from trolley poles to pantographs in March 1943 (Showa 18). Furthermore, a utility model right (Utility Model Registration No. 355463) for the viewger hardware was also obtained.
In June 1945 (Showa 20), the Sakuradote siding was prepared for the purpose of evacuating the electric trains, and they were dispersed and stored, including at Miyajima, to protect against war damage.

And then, on August 6, 1945 (Showa 20) at 8:15 AM, the first atomic bomb in human history was dropped on Hiroshima City. Humanity experienced unprecedented damage. The headquarters was partially destroyed by the atomic bombing. Among the Hiroden buildings in Hiroshima City, 50 out of 51 buildings were damaged, with the exception of one. At that time, there were 1,241 employees, of whom 185 died and 266 were injured. Among the streetcar vehicles, 108 out of the 123 in service were affected (22 completely burned, 3 partially burned, and 83 severely, moderately, or lightly damaged). The damage to the tracks extended over 28,150 meters.
章节.Past: Previously, there were the Miyajimaguchi Depot and the Koi Depot. Additionally, during the war, the Sakuradote Siding Line existed.
章节.Kōi Depot: It was abolished on October 25, 1960 (Showa 35) due to the improvement of the Ota River Floodway. Arate Depot was built as a replacement.
章节.Miyajimaguchi Depot: The siding line that runs parallel to the main line from Hiroden Miyajimaguchi Station to Miyajima Boat Racecourse is a remnant of the former Miyajimaguchi Depot.
章节.Sakuradote Branch Line: In June 1945 (Showa 20), it was constructed near the Kōryō Chūgaku-mae tram stop (present-day Kenbyō-mae tram stop).
章节.Recovery from the Atomic Bombing:
Shika City, on the Miyajima Line, train service resumed on the 7th, the day after the bombing, from Kusatsu Town (present-day Kusatsu) to Miyajima (present-day Hiroden Miyajimaguchi). On the following day, the 8th, service resumed on the entire line.
As for the city lines, with the cooperation of Hiroden employees and the military (40 members including the Tokyo Telegraph Unit), telephone poles were erected using trucks and ropes. The 300 poles owned by the Akatsuki Unit were also utilized, and telephone wires were pulled and repaired. Power was supplied from the Nijukashi Substation, and on August 9th, shuttle service resumed between Kibi and Nishitenmacho (present-day Tenmacho). The restoration was carried out on a single track. Since many male crew members had been conscripted into military service, female students from the Hiroshima Electric Railway Home Economics School performed duties as train conductors until the end of the war. The vehicles used at that time were two-car or three-car trains. When service resumed, passengers who had no fare were not forcibly asked to pay, and this action greatly encouraged the bewildered citizens. Restoration was completed as far as Konomachi on the 14th, just before the end of the war.

On August 9th, the vehicles that were used were the ones that a female student, who served as a conductor on the first train, testified about. Well then, regarding the 400 series TosaRe, a photograph taken by the Chugoku Shimbun on August 9th when operations resumed shows car 413. This is a record of the female students from "The Female Students Who Made the Trains Run," and then the 600 series. "The Town Where Hiroden Runs: Past and Present" and "Railway Pictorial August 2011 Special Issue" then became the 500 series cars 501 and 503.

After the war, restoration progressed, and at the Yoshida Depot, one 300 kW electric generator was used to restore the Chida Town Substation on August 18. Initially, restoration began with Kibi as the starting point: by August 19, it reached Dobashi; by the 21st, it reached Jūnichimachi; by the 23rd, it reached Sakankacho (present-day Honkawa-cho); and by September 7, it reached Hatchobori. Restoration also began from Hiroden Headquarters, reaching from Dentetsu-mae (present-day Hiroden Headquarters-mae) to Ujina (present-day Hiroshima Port) on August 18. By September 12, restoration reached Kayamachi, completing the entire Ujina Line. In December 1945 (Showa 20), the entire main line was restored. Subsequently, the Eba Line was restored in November 1947 (Showa 22), the Minami Line and Ujina Line in July 1948 (Showa 23), and the Yokogawa Line from Jūnichimachi to Yokogawa Bridge (present-day Betsuin-mae) on December 26. In July 1950 (Showa 25), the Miyajima Line was returned to double track. In March 1952 (Showa 27), the Shirajima Line was restored, though restoration was delayed due to road realignment.

The Chida-machi Substation resumed electrical supply on August 18, 1945. However, the Yasuragi-shita Substation, which was extremely close to the hypocenter, suffered catastrophic damage. As a result, the Chuo Substation was opened in front of the Honkawa-machi Tram Stop in November 1947 as a replacement.
Regarding the rolling stock, starting in 1948 (Showa 23), four remaining cars of the 100 series were converted into the 450 series, and all cars of the 500 series were converted into the 700 series (first generation). After the war, as restoration was not possible, the 300 series was scrapped in March 1951 (Showa 26).
At that time, some of the bombed vehicles are still preserved and operated today as A-bombed trams.

章节.Commencement of Through Services with th:
For the city line vehicles, in March 1951 (Showa 26), 10 cars of the 800 series (first generation) were introduced. In the same year, carbody renewal work on the 150 series also began. In September 1953 (Showa 28), 5 cars of the 500 series (second generation) were introduced. As a result, all cars of the 100 series (first generation) that had undergone renewal that year were scrapped. In March 1955 (Showa 30), 5 cars of the 550 series were introduced. Only car 551 adopted indirect control when it was originally manufactured and was permitted for direct through service on the Miyajima Line.
For the Miyajima Line vehicles, in February 1947 (Showa 22), 10 cars of the 1050 series were purchased from Keihan-Shin Kuko Dentetsu (now Hankyu Dentetsu). In 1954 (Showa 29), they were renewed with all-steel cars. In 1957 (Showa 32), the 1060 series was introduced. This became the last new high-floor cars, and the focus shifted to increasing the number of through-service-compatible cars.

Around 1955 (Showa 30), the Sanyo Main Line Ya route of JNR was competing with buses, and the Miyajima Line was struggling with a decline in passengers. This was because, at the time, the bus business was seeing an increase in passengers due to the extension of suburban routes. Previously, a connecting line had been constructed to allow maintenance of vehicles at the Chida Depot, but due to the land readjustment project associated with the improvement of the Ota River floodway in March 1957, it became necessary to relocate Kii Station and Nishi-Hiroshima Station. A plan was therefore made to create a direct service between the city lines and the Miyajima Line. A system was adopted whereby low-floor vehicles for the city lines would be run onto the line. Concurrently, low-floor platforms were installed at each station on the Miyajima Line, and the relocation of Kii Electric Tram Stop and Nishi-Hiroshima Station was completed in May 1957 (Showa 32). Starting in April 1958 (Showa 33), direct services began operating as chartered trains for groups. In January 1962 (Showa 37), regular services with 15-minute intervals commenced between Hiroshima Station and Hiroden-Hatsukaichi Station. Concurrently with the start of regular services, OriENtp

Each car body color is Venetian Red, with a stripe added, creating the "Direct Service Color." In May 1963 (Showa 38), the line was extended to Hiroden Miyajimaguchi Station.
Direct-service type cars were also added: Car 551 of the 550 series was named, and in March 1958 (Showa 33), three cars of the 850 series were introduced. Starting in 1960 (Showa 35), the 2000 series was introduced, followed by the 2500 series in 1961 (Showa 36). Regarding Car 2004, due to cost reduction efforts and Hiroden's challenging spirit, Nippon Sharyo Manufacturing produced the frame, and the company assembled its own steel car body, completing the work in November 1962 (Showa 37). Six cars of the 2000 series were manufactured by the end of the same year. Subsequently, cars of the 2500 series were also manufactured in the same manner.

Furthermore, improvements along the line also progressed, and the facilities of Rakurakuen Amusement Park were transferred to a separate company. Regarding the Miyajima area, in March 1958 (Showa 33), investment was made in Miyajima Matsudai Kankansen (currently Miyajima Matsudai Kisen). In April 1959 (Showa 34), Hiroshima Kanko Kaihatsu, a major shareholder of Hiroshima Electric Railway, opened the "Miyajima Ropeway." In 1965 (Showa 40), "Hiroden Miyajima Garden," which currently operates "etto," was established.
章节.A Moving Train Museum:
In the 1950s and 1960s, similar to other cities with streetcars, Hiroshima Electric Railway also faced the same situation—along with the advancement of the automobile system, traffic congestion increased, making it difficult to maintain scheduled operations. As a result, passenger numbers declined, leading to a decrease in revenue, and the company was forced to confront the issue of whether to continue operations or discontinue them. Once, in June 1963 (Showa 38), permission was granted for vehicles to enter the track area. Around that time, there was also a plan for a subway in Hiroshima City, which was intended as a transition. However, at that time, officials from Hiroshima Electric Railway continued to persuade the city and the police department, while simultaneously, the Hiroshima Prefectural Police also dispatched an independent investigation team to the six areas where streetcars were still numerous at the time to conduct investigations. What they found was that, as a method to alleviate congestion in the central area, the streetcar had been entrusted with a new role and had evolved. In February 1971 (Showa 46), Hiroden issued a "Save the Streetcars" declaration, shifting its policy toward preserving the streetcars. As a result, without changing the alternative transportation systems,

If the route were abolished, it would lead to a deterioration of the traffic environment in the central area; therefore, the ban on motor vehicles entering the track area, which had been temporarily lifted, was successfully reinstated in December 1971 (Showa 46). Subsequently, measures such as a citywide total parking ban, installation of priority signals for trams, and installation of right-turn lanes were implemented. By acquiring vehicles from the abolished operator, the two-axle single-unit cars were replaced with bogie cars, enabling larger vehicles and one-man operation. Efforts were also made to increase speed: in March 1974 (Showa 49), priority signals for trams were introduced for the first time near Kaigan-dori, and in February 1975 (Showa 50), the system was extended from Minamimachi 6-chome to Ujina 5-chome. Through organizational reforms and rationalization, one-man operation began on the Shirajima Line in 1969 (Showa 44). By 1976 (Showa 51), the city lines had adopted one-man operation except during rush hours. Thanks to these efforts, it was barely possible to continue operations. During this period, in 1971 (Showa 46)

On the 2nd, the old Line 7 was abolished, as it ran from Hiroshima Station via Kamiyamacho to Yokokawa Station. Additionally, because the central part of Hiroshima City is located in a delta at the mouth of the Ota River, issues related to groundwater veins and geology made large-scale subway construction difficult with the technology available at the time, which was also a factor in avoiding its abolition.

On the city lines, from 1966 (Showa 41), the Osaka Municipal Streetcar acquired cars 750 and Bi900, and in 1971 (Showa 46), it acquired cars 570, Bi1100, and 1150 from the Kobe Municipal Streetcar. As a result, the two-axle single trucks remaining on the Hiroden were replaced. In 1966 (Showa 41), all cars of the 200 series (first generation) were scrapped; in 1969 (Showa 44), all cars of the 400 and 450 series were scrapped; and in 1971, all cars of the 150 series were scrapped. All two-axle single trucks were scrapped, completing the transition to larger vehicles. Additionally, among the bogie cars, all cars of the 600 series (first generation) were scrapped in 1972 (Showa 47). Four cars of the 700 series (first generation) were scrapped by 1972 (Showa 47), and nine cars of the 800 series (first generation) were scrapped by 1976 (Showa 51).

On the Miyajima Line, in 1967 (Showa 42), 1070 series cars were purchased from Keihan-Shin-Kyuko Electric Railway. In 1977 (Showa 52), 1080 series cars were purchased from Keihan-Shin-Kyuko Electric Railway. In 1982 (Showa 57), 1050 series cars were modified into 1090 series cars. At the same time, the scrapping of wooden cars also progressed: in 1966 (Showa 41), all 1020 series cars were scrapped; in 1968 (Showa 43), all 1010 series cars were scrapped, and all wooden cars were retired.
The larger-scale direct through service cars also progressed. From 1973 to 1974, a total of eight 2000 series cars, excluding one odd-numbered car, were modified into two-car coupled units.

In 1975 (Showa 50), a fire occurred at Nishida Depot, resulting in some vehicles being scrapped. To replenish them, 600 series cars were purchased from the Nishitetsu Kitakyushu Line, and one 800 series (first generation) car, which had been retired, underwent one-man operation conversion. Starting in 1978 (Showa 53), 1900 series cars were purchased from the Kyoto City Tram, along with which the 700 series (first generation) and 800 series (first generation) were completely retired, and some 750 series cars were also scrapped.
In 1979 (Showa 54), operation of the three-car articulated 3000 series began. The 3000 series was Hiroden's first three-car articulated train, measuring 7 meters longer than conventional models, with a capacity of 180 passengers, an increase of 50 compared to earlier types. Additionally, two-car articulated cars 1101, 1201, and 1301 series were purchased and modified from the Nishitetsu Fukuoka City Line, which had been discontinued in 1976 (Showa 51). Furthermore, with some minor modifications, the 1301 series had been in service as the 1300 series since 1976.

After that, in order to increase the number of through services, the 2500 series two-car articulated trains, which had been mainly used on the city lines at the time, were converted into three-car articulated trains starting in 1985 (Showa 60) and became the 3100 series. Additionally, one of the two Ho-Mu cars for the Miyajima Line at Hiroden Nishi-Hiroshima Station was modified for through service use, bringing the number of Ho-Mu cars for through services to three.

Initially, when the 750 series cars were transferred, they were repainted in Hiroden colors. However, from the time of transfers such as the 900 series onward, in order to cut costs, they were operated without repainting to their pre-transfer livery. Additionally, rather than doing so, Osaka City and Kobe City procured inexpensive exterior paints and so on, maintaining the previous paintwork. From there, they came to be known by nicknames such as “the Moving Electric Car Museum” and “the Streetcar Museum” among fans. Initially, when this nickname was coined, Hiroden disliked the name and held a public contest for a new livery, but due to opposition from the local design council, the repainting was abandoned. On the other hand, as a service to passengers, they actively implemented measures such as enlarging the destination displays and retrofitting air conditioning, and did not insist on preserving the original form.

Furthermore, on the sides of the transferred cars, a “transfer plate” has been affixed, indicating the former operator and the year of transfer, dating back to February 20, 1979 (Showa 54).

Furthermore, as no vehicles had been introduced from abroad, in 1977 (Showa 52), on the 65th anniversary of the line's opening, discussions arose about introducing vehicles from abroad. Since the track gauge was the same at 1,435 mm, it was possible to operate in both directions with cabs fitted. Therefore, rather than using surplus vehicles from the line's underground conversion, it was decided to introduce used vehicles from Dortmund, Germany. Including a vehicle purchase cost of 5 million yen, transportation costs of 15 million yen, and modification costs of 25 million yen per trainset, seven 70-series cars were transferred from that city in 1981 (Showa 56). In addition, to commemorate the sister-city relationship between Hiroshima City and Hanover, Germany, Hiroshima City sent a tea room as a return gift, and in 1989 (Heisei 1), the 200-series (second generation) (commonly known as the "Hanover Train") was presented. Hiroshima Electric Railway has also donated vehicles abroad; in 1986 (Showa 61), car 578 was donated to the city of San Francisco.

In 1988 (Showa 63), car 3103 was painted with a spray painting by the West German artist Jo—Brockelhof and named “Peace Burn.” In 1992 (Heisei 4), due to deterioration of the paint, a full repainting was considered, but around August, only the waist area was repainted while the rest was stripped and changed to a different color. In August 1995 (Heisei 7), a complete repainting was carried out.
Additionally, starting in 1972 (Showa 47), the “Train Approach Device” was gradually installed at tram stops. Building on this development, the “Train Lock System” was experimentally adopted between Hiroshima Station and Kibi in 1980 (Showa 55). By March 1985 (Showa 60), it had been installed at all tram stops. Furthermore, measures were taken such as equipping tram stops with guidance systems that broadcast train operating status, safety fences, roofs, and flat safety zones in an island-like configuration to ensure the safety of users at the stops.
章节.Introduction of Light Rail Vehicles:
In 1980 (Showa 55), the 3500 series was introduced as the first new cars in a long time. These became the Keikai Electric Trains. Initially, they were owned by the development committee, but in 1981 (Showa 56), Hiroden purchased them. From 1982 (Showa 57) onward, used motors from scrapped vehicles were also utilized for the 700 series Keikai Electric Trains (second generation). From 1983 (Showa 58) onward, the 800 series (second generation) was introduced, followed by the 3700 series in 1984 (Showa 59), the 3800 series in 1987 (Showa 62), the 3900 series in 1990 (Heisei 2), and the 3950 series in 1997 (Heisei 9). The 3800 series was unusual for its time, as it adopted VVV inverter control.

On the Miyajima Line, No. cars underwent updates such as permanent coupling of the 1050 series, replacement of trucks, and installation of large destination displays, and in 1982 (Showa 57), the 1090 series was renumbered. In 1984 (Showa 59), air-conditioning modifications were also carried out on the only dedicated cars for the Miyajima Line. Due to an increase in through-service cars, scrappings progressed: in 1980 (Showa 55), all 1040 series cars were scrapped; in 1985 (Showa 60), all 1030 series cars were scrapped; in 1987 (Showa 62), all 1070 series cars were scrapped; in 1989 (Heisei 1), all 1060 and 1080 series cars were scrapped; and in 1991 (Heisei 3), all 1090 series cars were scrapped, bringing an end to all Miyajima Line dedicated cars, which had been called “high-floor cars.”
Furthermore, in 1971 (Showa 46), two-axle single-unit cars were reintroduced after being completely scrapped. In 1984 (Showa 59), coinciding with the local event “Sun Sun Hiroshima,” the 100 series, restored to its state at the time of the line’s opening, made its appearance. In 1987 (Showa 62), the 150 series was reinstated as a bomb-damaged train.

With the introduction of the Keikai Electric Train No., the aging 570 and 750 series trains were gradually retired in large numbers. The 900 series, which had not undergone air-conditioning modifications, also saw retirements. Except for a few single cars that were preserved until the late 1990s, the air-conditioning work was completed.
In 1994 (Heisei 6), the 70 series was introduced during rush hours. Excluding through services, this marked the first introduction of articulated vehicles on the city line. Subsequently, the operating range of the articulated vehicles was gradually expanded.
Introduction of low-floor vehicles (LRV) and retirement of conventional vehicles
In 1990 (Heisei 2), following a study tour of Europe and amid a rapid reassessment of streetcars, efforts were actively undertaken to transition to LRT, aiming for a new era of public transportation.

The lightweight electric train WosaraNi was evolved; barrier-free compliant ultra-low-floor trains had been considered since the 1990s, taking a lead—Roppa's main vehicle models—were compatible with Japan's climate, but the possibility of 100% low-floor vehicles was questioned. As of the year before the additional procurement of the 3950 series, Alna Koki, Sumitomo Metal Industries, and Toyo Denki Seizo had conducted studies, but because reducing the floor height from 79 cm to 75 cm was the limit regardless of cost, the introduction of domestically produced low-floor trains was once abandoned. Therefore, the policy shifted to importing from manufacturers abroad that had already pioneered practical applications. Adtranz, Siemens, and Alstom were considered, and starting in 1999 (Heisei 11), the GREEN MOVER 5000 series manufactured by Germany's Siemens was introduced. Because the completion of the 5000 series was delayed and shipping by sea would have caused the arrival date to exceed the government's subsidy payment deadline, a large transport aircraft (An-124) was used.

Air transport. Hiroshima Airport was widely reported in the mass media as a gathering place for railway fans and aviation fans. This vehicle has received the Barrier-Free Promotion Merit Award and the Chief Cabinet Secretary Award.
After that, due to problems such as increased transportation costs when using vehicles from outside Japan, high costs and long lead times when importing parts, and the fact that the vehicle structures did not take Japanese operations into account, the "U3 Project" was launched in 2001 (Heisei 13), and development of domestically produced low-floor vehicles began. From 2004 (Heisei 16), the first domestically produced 100% ultra-low-floor train, the Green Mover MAX 5100 series, was introduced, and on December 19 of the same year, it was delivered to the Eba Depot (Eba, Nakaku, Hiroshima City). Additionally, auxiliary steps (footrests) are being installed at the entrances and exits of existing vehicles, aiming to create public transportation suitable for an aging society.

In order to introduce soReraNo's ultra-low-floor vehicles, the disposal of aging self-owned original vehicles and transferred vehicles from other cities is progressing, resulting in the disappearance of the original 500 series, 550 series, and former Kobe 1100 series. All vehicles of the 2000 series (self-owned) have withdrawn from revenue service, while only one vehicle each remains of the 570 series (former Kobe), 600 series (former Kitakyushu), and 1150 series (former Kobe). The 650 series (self-owned, bomb-damaged vehicles), which had previously only seen vehicles written off due to accidents, also saw two vehicles withdrawn from service (car 653 is out of service and stored at Eboshi Depot, while car 654 was scrapped and is preserved at the Hiroshima City Transportation Science Museum), and the generational replacement has progressed. Unlike the 650 series, which received media coverage and held retirement ceremonies, most vehicles are being taken out of service, scrapped, or dismantled without any confirmation of issues with the replacement vehicles.

In March 2000 (Heisei 12), barrier-free access was implemented at Ni-Takano Bridge Station. Subsequently, similar construction work is being carried out at other tram stops. In 2003 (Heisei 15), Yokokawa Station was renovated. In conjunction with this, the Tokaichi connecting line was improved, and Route 7 was revived as a service heading toward Hiroden Headquarters Front. In the same year, in conjunction with the completion of a new passenger terminal at Hiroshima Port Tram Stop, the route was extended by 100 meters, and the station was relocated.
章节.Since 2010:
On April 11, 2011 (Heisei 23), due to the city line timetable revision, Line 3 operated between Hiroden Nishi-Hiroshima and Hiroshima Port during the morning rush hour. Subsequently, during that time period, the service was shortened to operate between Hiroden Nishi-Hiroshima and Ujina 2-chome (as of the April 2, 2018 timetable revision, Line 3 resumed operating between Hiroden Nishi-Hiroshima and Hiroshima Port for most services, excluding nighttime services). Due to the city line timetable revision on July 11, 2011, Line 5 generally operated between Hiroshima Station and Hiroshima Port, with services running at 12-minute intervals during the day.
It was reported that in 2011 (Heisei 23), aiming for full-scale implementation from fiscal 2013 (Heisei 25) onward, a social experiment for a credence-based fare system would begin. From February 15 to March 31, 2012 (Heisei 24), IC Leader validators for alighting were installed on the middle doors of the three-car articulated trains (cars 3703 and 3906), and a social experiment was conducted allowing users of ICKa—Do (PASPY and ICOCA) to board and alight through all doors.

In August 2012 (Heisei 24), it was announced that an increase in fares from around 20 yen to 30 yen would be considered in conjunction with the renewal of low-floor vehicles and the renovation of the Ya tram stop. As of November of the same year, it was then announced that a fare increase would be implemented in 2013.
According to a report in the Chugoku Shimbun dated November 23, 2012, new three-car ultra-low-floor vehicles were planned to be introduced on the Shirajima Line starting in February 2013 (Heisei 25), and would operate as a through service between the Shirajima Line and the Eba Line. In a Hiroden press release dated December 18, 2012, it was announced that two two-car formations (cars 1001 and 1002) would debut on February 14, 2013, with one of them receiving a tie-up wrap. Commercial operation of these ultra-low-floor vehicles of the 1000 series (second generation) began on February 15, 2013.

Based on the “Hiroden Service Improvement Plan” formulated in May 2012 (Heisei 24), continuous efforts have been made, such as introducing 1000-series ultra-low-floor vehicles, making tram stops barrier-free, and upgrading the route guidance system.
On January 8, 2013 (Heisei 25), the former president was dismissed for unilaterally carrying out business operations and thereby obstructing legitimate duties. The new president has decided to cancel certain projects up to that point, including the Ekimae Ohashi Line improvement plan using an underground method and the fare increase announced in November 2012.
Subsequently, on December 13, 2013 (Heisei 25), an application was submitted to revise fares in line with the consumption tax increase in April 2014 (Heisei 26). The application proposed a 10-yen increase for city line fares, keeping railway line fares unchanged, and increasing the combined railway-tram fare by raising the tram portion by 20 yen. The revision was approved on March 4, 2014 (Heisei 26) and took effect on April 1 of the same year.
章节.Bus Business:
The Hiroshima Electric Railway NoBus business has been managed by the Bus Business Headquarters since January 2014, and under it are the Urban Area Transport Sales Department, Regional Transport Sales Department, Kure Transport Sales Department, and Bus Planning Department. Centered in Hiroshima City, it operates general route buses in western Hiroshima Prefecture and Kure City, in addition to operating express buses to Hiroshima Airport and various locations in the San'in region (Tottori City and Yonago City in Tottori Prefecture, and Matsue City, Hamada City, and Masuda City in Shimane Prefecture). It is also known as Aoba Bus.
The operating mileage is 1,404.6 km (as of March 31, 2016), an increase of approximately 200 km compared to the 1,191.9 km operating mileage in fiscal 2011 (Heisei 23) before the integration with the Kure City Transportation Bureau.
The group companies engaged in the bus business include Eiichi-Di—Nishi-Hiroshima (Bus), Hokuhoku Kotsu, and Geiyo Bus.

In order to adjust the bus routes competing with the Hiroden Electric Railway's routes, Hiroden acquired a majority stake in Hiroshima Noriai Jidosha Co., Ltd., which was established in 1928 (Showa 3), in 1929 (Showa 4), making it a subsidiary and entering into its management. This was to adjust the routes competing with the electric railway. Furthermore, to prevent other companies from entering the areas along the Miyajima Line, Hiroden initially operated them directly, but with the start of its bus business, it merged with Hiroshima Noriai Jidosha in 1938 (Showa 13), established an automobile division, and integrated the businesses. By November 5, 1942 (Showa 17), during the wartime period, business integration of the bus operations was carried out with seven companies (Sandankyō Jidosha, Ota Jidosha, Heiwa Jidosha, Marusan Jidosha, Minouchi Jidosha Shōkai, Kumano Kozue Jidosha, and Hiroshima Kōgai Jidosha) as well as one individual.

After that, Geiyo Bus became a subsidiary of Bibai Kotsu, and Hiroshima Bus became a subsidiary (after that, it received a recommendation from the Fair Trade Commission and sold more than half of its shares). EIchi・Di—Nishi-Hiroshima (Bon Bus) was spun off, the company withdrew from chartered bus services, and it obtained the first Green Management Certification in the Chugoku-Shikoku region. After taking over the bus business of Kure City Transportation Bureau, it became the largest bus operator in the Chugoku region as of 2013 (Heisei 25).
Regarding bus vehicles, as of March 2018, it owned 564 units. Before the merger, as of March 2011, it owned 410 units from Hiroden and 163 units from Kure City Transportation Bureau, so the number increased by roughly the amount of transferred vehicles.

As of the end of March 2018, there are 564 Nouchi vehicles, 26 Hybrid Busga vehicles, 42 CNGBusga vehicles, 247 vehicles that comply with the latest NOx emission regulations, and 432 vehicles equipped with an idling stop function. Additionally, under the "Hiroden Service Improvement Plan," efforts are being made to enhance services, such as replacing seats with "Hiroden Original" seats and introducing non-step buses.
章节.Route Overview: The number of tram stops includes temporary stations. Additionally, the Kamiyamachi Tram Stop is counted as one stop when combining Kamiyamachi-Higashi and Kamiyamachi-Nishi.
章节.Extension to the Dejima Area: In April 2019, reports were made regarding a route extension plan for the currently under-construction reclaimed land area in the Dejima district of Minami-ku, Hiroshima City. The plan involves extending the current Ujina Line by 1.2 km from Hiroshima Port Station, its present terminus, to the southern side of Hiroshima Municipal Hiroshima Special Support School, where a new vehicle depot will be constructed as the new terminus. Construction is expected to begin after fiscal year 2024, once the land reclamation is completed.
章节.Elimination of the Main Line Crank:
Hiroshima Electric Railway announced a plan in September 1997 (Heisei 9) to apply for a license to construct a new line connecting Hiroshima Station and Hiroden Nishi-Hiroshima Station, via Heiwa-dori, Ekimae-dori, and Ekimae Ohashi. The section between Hiroshima Station and Hiroden Nishi-Hiroshima Station is currently served by Line 2, but the route includes a sharp bend at an intersection, which has become a challenge for operating long trains. Heiwa-dori is exceptionally wide, providing ample space for laying double tracks. This would allow the bend to be avoided, enabling high-speed operation between terminals with longer train formations and significantly improving convenience.

Immediately after the announcement, several rounds of negotiations were held between Hiroshima City, citizens, and the Transport Council. At the time, Hiroshima City desired the construction of an east-west line via the Astram Line. However, Hiroshima City was facing a massive fiscal deficit and had embarked on large-scale projects such as the construction of a new stadium. Coupled with the substantial deficits of the existing Astram Line and the national policy to promote the LRT conversion of streetcars, the public transportation development plan was revised to focus on improving existing streetcars and buses. Furthermore, Hiroshima Electric Railway submitted several revised proposals (the final proposal being the construction of only the section from Saikanonmachi Tram Stop at the western end of Heiwa-dori to the Eboshi Line) by around 2002 (Heisei 14). However, as no financial prospects emerged for covering costs such as the replacement of Midori Ohashi Bridge, the plan was shelved.
章节.Others:
Event 
Every year, around June 10th, the "Tram Matsuri" is held. Additionally, various events are held, such as the running of Tanabata Trams or Christmas Trams.
章节.Railway Musume: Tomi-Tech is primarily responsible for developing the Railway Musume series, and as characters for Hiroshima Electric Railway, there are two characters: "Takano Miyuki" (first appeared in the regular series, vol. 3) and "Tokiba Marina" (first appeared in the station poster series, vol. 5). The Railway Musume station poster vol. 5 (Takano Miyuki & Tokiba Marina) was displayed at tram stops and stations, promoting barrier-free access and the prevention of in-train accidents.
章节.Honorary Consuls of the Federal Republic: On May 28, 2001, Ni, along with Okubo Oo, then Representative Director and Chairman, was appointed as the "Honorary Consul of the Federal Republic of Germany in Hiroshima." On February 14, 2007, Ota Tetsuya, then Representative Director and President, succeeded him. While Ota was still alive, as of September 14, 2011, his name was listed by the German Embassy; however, after Ota's death, as of November 18, 2011, the German Embassy removed his name from the list, and on December 19 of the same year, he was also removed from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' "List of Foreign Diplomatic Missions in Japan." Previously, an Honorary Consulate office had been established within the Hiroshima Electric Railway headquarters, and its jurisdiction covered Hiroshima Prefecture.
章节.Removal of President Ochi: On January 8, 2013 (Heisei 25), Hide Nobu Ochi was demoted from Representative Director and President to Director. Masao Murata, Executive Officer, assumed the position of President. This was effectively a dismissal, with the stated reason being “that Representative Director Ochi’s unilateral execution of business operations was causing problems for the company’s organizational structure.” No detailed explanation of the reasons was provided. The extraordinary board of directors meeting was held with Ochi absent as an outside director, while all full-time officers attended. Subsequently, Murata, who had become President, clarified that Ochi’s reasons for dismissal—such as his public announcement of plans like fare increases and the new Hiroshima Station Front Line without consulting the board of directors—would be reviewed, including potentially reverting those plans to a blank slate.
章节.Location shooting for the TV drama \"Sei: In the 1982 television drama *Nippon TV Drama "Nibu Keisatsu PART-II"*, episode 18, "Hiroshima City Panic!!", Hiroden Electric Railway cooperated with the filming. During the filming period, train services on various lines in the city center were temporarily suspended, and nearby roads were temporarily closed for the shoot. For the filming of the climax scene, the company's own 750 series car 766 was operated to Hiroden Miyajima Station (now Hiroden Miyajimaguchi Station), where an explosion was staged on the station premises (at that time). At the moment of the explosion, the surrounding area briefly experienced a power outage. The footage from this scene was also reused in the opening sequence of *Nibu Keisatsu PART-III*. The car had already been slated for retirement. For the purpose of the filming, its livery and advertisements were changed from those of the "Pearl Rice" service that had ended its commercial operation. It was then repainted as the "Nishiki-do" car, sponsored by the same company for the program, and was officially retired after the explosion scene. This episode also featured shots of the operating control room and the head office building as they appeared at the time. Additionally, the filming was discussed in the reader submissions section of the magazine *Tetsudo Fan*.
章节.Hiring of Female Train and Bus Drivers: The number of female train operators and bus drivers is increasing, but amid this trend, former employees of Hiroden Kanko, which withdrew from the charter bus business, can also be seen working as bus guides.
章节.Support Activities for Athletes: In 2011, than the season, Hiroshima Gas-affiliated No Snowboard Alpine skier Tomika Takeuchi to the sponsor of the World Snowboard Federation.
章节.Support for Light Rail Projects in Tochi: In March 2023, aiming for the opening of the No. line, the Tochigi Prefecture's Utsunomiya City is advancing the light rail project. In response to a request for support from the mayor of Utsunomiya and others in 2015, Hiroden President Murata replied, "We will provide comprehensive cooperation," and expressed the intention that support is possible in terms of technology, crew training, and other areas. Masatoshi Nakao, a former Hiroden executive, assumed the position of director of Utsunomiya Light Rail, which will serve as the operating entity, in November of the same year. Since January 2021, four prospective crew members from Utsunomiya Light Rail have been dispatched to Hiroden for training.
章节.Other Related Companies, Organizations,:
School Corporation Suzumine Gakuen (Suzumine Women's Junior College, Suzumine Women's Middle School, and Suzumine Women's High School)
  The foundation Hiroshima Gas Denki Gakuen was established in 1940, and even after the war, many directors and council members from Hiroshima Gas occupied positions. However, due to the declining birthrate, the future prospects of school management became uncertain. In response, Ota Tetsuya, who was then the representative director of our company and also served as a director for both Shudo Gakuen and Suzumine Gakuen, took the lead in initiating discussions on merging the two school corporations, and an agreement on the corporate merger was reached in 2013. In April 2015, the merger was completed through Suzumine Gakuen's absorption by Shudo Gakuen. Meanwhile, the board of directors of Shudo Gakuen is composed mainly of key members from the "Nibakai" group, a circle of influential figures from Hiroshima's business community, including our company and Hiroshima Gas.
  Furthermore, although there is no direct relationship with Suzumine Gakuen, a vocational school called Hiroshima Dentetsu Home Economics Girls' School was also established during the war with the aim of securing personnel for train operations.

英文.全文:
Overview
The head office is located at 2-9-29 Higashichida-cho, Nakaku, Hiroshima City, Hiroshima Prefecture. The current company was established on April 10, 1942 (Showa 17) through separation from Hiroshima Gas Electric Railway (see "Corporate History" for details). It is the largest streetcar operator in Japan and the largest bus operator in the Chugoku-Shikoku region. As of 2012 (Heisei 24), streetcars, buses, and real estate have become the three main pillars of Hiroden. Hiroden buses are commonly referred to as "Ao Bus."
For electronic money (transportation-type IC cards), PASPY, issued by the Hiroshima Prefecture Bus Association, can be used. It can also be used at affiliated companies such as Eiichi-Dai Nishi Hiroshima, Geiyo Bus, Bihoku Kotsu, Miyajima Matsudai Kisen, and Miyajima Ropeway. Additionally, ICOCA of West Japan Railway Company (JR West) can be used with PASPY. Other transportation-type IC cards such as Suica and PASMO can also be used.

The company motto is "Cooperation and unity, service from the heart, zero accidents." Additionally, the "Hiroshima Electric Railway Employee Code of Conduct" has been established, which includes the pledge "Zero Accidents." The slogan is "Aiming to be a company that is kind to people and the environment." Furthermore, "serving the local community" is also a key theme.
Before making a full-scale entry into the real estate business, as part of the development along the Miyajima Line, development was carried out in Rakurakuen before World War II, and in Fujitsurien in 1955 (Showa 30).
On October 28, 1958 (Showa 33), Ginrin Fudosan was established as a subsidiary. On October 31, 1959 (Showa 34), the "Hiroden Building" was completed in Kamiyamacho, marking entry into the office building rental business. On February 1, 1961 (Showa 36), Hiroden Fudosan was established, and the "Second Hiroden Building" was constructed in Hatchobori. On October 1, 1971 (Showa 46), Ginrin Fudosan and Hiroden Fudosan merged, with Hiroden Fudosan continuing as the surviving company.

In 1960 (Showa 35), along with the No Economic Policy Income Doubling Plan, the sale of housing No increased. In 1967 (Showa 42), a Development Section was established within the Business Division. The company then fully entered the real estate business. On July 16, 1969 (Showa 44), the Development Department was expanded, and the "Real Estate Department," which became the predecessor of the Real Estate Business Headquarters, was newly established. Starting from the 1970 (Showa 45) fiscal year, it came to cover the deficits of the railway division and the bus division.
Initially, small-scale housing development was carried out. Beginning with the development of eight buildings in Nakachi (present-day Saeki Ward, Yahata Higashi) in 1969 (Showa 44), five buildings were developed in Jōnai (present-day Hatsukaichi City, Jōnai) in 1970 (Showa 45), and Hara (present-day Hatsukaichi City, Hara) was also developed.

After that, the company fully entered residential complex development, selling 553 lots of “Kannon-dai” in 1970 (Showa 45), 188 lots of “Tsukimi-dai” in 1971 (Showa 46), 956 lots of “Yoko-dai” in 1972 (Showa 47), and from 1973 (Showa 48), 63 units of Suikodai Complex (currently Kuchida 5-chome). From 1974 (Showa 49) onward, it eventually began selling “Bishamon-dai,” which comprised more than 2,500 lots. In 1979, it sold 357 lots of Hiroden Koi Complex. In 1986 (Showa 61), it acquired 224 lots for a land readjustment project complex called “Higashi-Kannon-dai Complex.” In 1991 (Heisei 3), it acquired 127 lots for another land readjustment project complex called “Amenity Town Nihonminami.” In 2010, it sold 63 units of “Ujina Mikou.”

The company has developed mansions such as "Rakurakuen Mansion" in 1975 (Showa 50), "View Heights Kifue" in 1989 (Heisei 1), and "Grand Sociale Itsukaichi" in 1999 (Heisei 11). Additionally, in 2004, it developed Miyajima, and in 2008, it developed the Saijo Station Front residential project.
Subsequent developments were not limited to areas along railway lines but also included areas along bus routes.
Afterward, although the railway and bus divisions improved their profitability and eliminated deficits, the company continued to engage in leasing office buildings in areas such as Kamiya-cho, as well as selling and brokering residential land and mansions for general use.
In 2012 (Heisei 24), the Hiroden Building and other structures were rebuilt, and "Hiroshima Tramvaire Building D" ("Tramvaire" means "green train" in French) opened.

History of the Company
The current company was established on April 10, 1942 (Showa 17) by separating the transportation business from "Hiroshima Gas Electric Railway Co., Ltd." (currently Hiroshima Gas). Including its predecessor company, it was established on June 18, 1910 (Meiji 43) as "Hiroshima Electric Railway Co., Ltd."

At the time of its founding as Hiroshima Electric Railway Co., Ltd., it was a company established under similar circumstances to those of a company under the Obayashi Group. Furthermore, at a certain point, these two companies merged into one as "Hiroshima Gas Electric Railway Co., Ltd." Yoshigoro Obayashi, the head of the Obayashi Group, released Hiroshima Gas shares between 1913 (Taisho 2) and 1914 (Taisho 3) to support Kitahama Bank after its collapse. In 1916 (Taisho 6), following Yoshigoro Obayashi's death, his successor, Yoshio Obayashi, inherited the shares, but the position of president remained vacant, leading to the company's departure from the Obayashi Group. Both companies received support from Suzuki Shoten, and their shares were sold to the entrepreneur Kenichi Fujita. At the same time, as the same person served as president of both, due to differences in demand between natural gas and streetcars, they merged with Hiroshima Gas.

The head office location was established at this site since the founding of Hiroshima Electric Railway at the time of its opening. However, during the final stage of the Pacific War, in 1945 (Showa 20), after the atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima City, the head office was moved to Rakurakuen, Saeki Ward, Hiroshima City, by August 30 of the following year. Additionally, during the era of Hiroshima Gas Electric Railway, the head office was also located at the current site in Otemachi, Naka Ward, Hiroshima City.

The Hiroshima Gas Electric Railway Gakuen, a public interest incorporated foundation established during the Hiroshima Gas integration era, was reorganized and renamed to the Suzumine Gakuen school corporation (which operated Suzumine Women's Junior College, Suzumine Women's Middle and High School [now Hiroshima Shudo University Hiroshima Kuso Middle and High School]) after the Pacific War. As of March 31, 2012, among the nine directors and supervisors of the Gakuen, five were affiliated with Hiroden and Hiroshima Gas. In April 2015, it was absorbed and merged into the Shudo Gakuen school corporation. Furthermore, as a remnant of the Hiroshima Gas integration era, the Hiroshima Electric Railway health insurance association continues to be jointly operated with Hiroshima Gas under the name "Hiroshima Gas Electric Railway Health Insurance Association."

From the end of 1955 to 1967, as one of the companies jointly investing in the professional baseball team Hiroshima Carp (now Hiroshima Toyo Carp), the president of Hiroden at the time also served as the president of the team.

As of 1998, the train business had a profit of approximately 600 million yen, although the bus business recorded a deficit of over 1 billion yen. These were offset, so the company as a whole remained nearly profitable thanks to its real estate business. To reform this situation, a company system was implemented internally starting in December 1998, with the reform of the bus business in mind. The railway and track business was handled by the Train Company, the bus business by the Bus Company, and the real estate business by the Real Estate Company, while general affairs, accounting, and other functions were managed by the M&S Company. In April 2012, the Kure City-operated bus routes were taken over, and thus the Kure Bus Company was established to handle this responsibility. The internal company system was abolished in January 2014 due to an organizational restructuring, and the company transitioned to a headquarters system. The railway and track business is now managed by the Train Business Headquarters, the bus business by the Bus Business Headquarters, and the real estate business by the Real Estate Business Headquarters.
